text_fidelity_a:
Jabra Evolve 65t True Wireless Bluetooth Earbuds, UC Optimized – Superior Call Quality and Connectivity – Passive Noise Cancelling Earbuds with up to 15 hours of Battery Life with Charging Case When reviewing headsets, I don't just pop them on and hit play on a favorite song or take a call. I actually run them through a battery of sound tests from an audio site. I run all sets through the same test to make it fair. First on my PC and then on my iPhone XS. I find it's the best way to make an unbiased review.
• Bass: Poor with a limited range. It also wasn’t balanced between the earbuds.
• High freq: Better than the bass, but still a limited range. It was balanced between the earbuds much better though.
• Rattle: None, but it would be weird if earbuds rattled. Ok that’s not true, I stepped on a pair at the gym that rattled afterwards. Oops.
• Volume: Sufficient. I don’t blast my earbuds, because I like to keep my hearing. I could turn it low enough to not hear, and loud enough to be uncomfortable.
• Clarity: Isolated for the sound test they did fine. However, outside the site the clarity started to degrade, and on a call was bad enough to be an issue.

The sound check results were mediocre. Bass was lacking, as was the general range of the set. These actually did worse than their cheaper behind the neck set (Jabra Evolve 65e UC).

As for things other than sound, like usability I like to ask myself what I’m looking for and if product meets those expectations. So, here goes:

Would these last the entire workday?
Yes and No, if you take them off to charge during lunch then you will probably be fine. Otherwise no they are going to die out about 75% through a standard 8 hr workday. They require a USB port and their little case thing to charge. I had no issues as long as I remember to charge them at lunch.

Are they easy to use?
The basics, yes. All the extra features, not so much. I opened the box up and was happy to see the quick-start guide, unfortunately if there is a manual I didn't get one. I found a digital copy tucked away in the iPhone app, but nothing in the box itself. That made anything past the basics in the quick-start guide a matter of trial and error, until I found the manual tucked away in the App. For the price, that seems like a rather cheap move. There is a ton of useful info in the manual that is not contained in the quick-start guide.

Can I take calls seamlessly?
Yes, but for me at least the call experience was lacking. The voices on some but not all calls were a bit muddled, however they could hear me just fine. So poor marks for the sound quality, but high marks for the mic.
Speaking of mics, can I mute the mic easily?
Easily, yes. But knowing for sure if you are muted (we've all been there) only when using the computer dongle, on my iPhone using Bluetooth, eek not so much. Had to leave it to faith. That was a bit scary.

Plays music well (aka does it have range and bass)?
Meh. I have the sound review at the top. As you can imagine, lack of bass negatively impacts listening to music. I mean it wasn’t awful but it wasn’t great either.

Can I opt to hear people talking to me (audio pass-through)?
Yes, but it sounds super static and buzzy. The sound is not clear and crisp at all. Also, you can't just pop an earbud out and listen with one ear. If the earbuds are anymore than head-width apart they stop working all together. According to the manual, you should be able to use the right earbud by itself, but that was not my experience. It also would stop working (although it worked a bit longer than the left) once they were too far apart.

Noise-canceling abilities, can I at least block out the cubical next to me?
Sort of. You can block drumming blah blah blah sounds, but ringing phones and coworkers talking, not so much. Although it did take the edge off. The Jabra iPhone app for these has some cool ambient sound machine settings, waves crashing, thunderstorm, white noise, etc. Probably my favorite thing about this whole set.

Are they comfortable?
I didn't like them, but I am a petite human and have small ears. I also don't like the weird vacuuming pressure you feel when wearing anything noise-cancelling. I will give these neutral marks for comfort, I think if you had larger ear canals and didn't mind closed type headsets these would probably be fine.

Are these worth the price?
Nope. For the price these should be spectacular and check all the boxes. They are mediocre in sound quality even though they are packed with features. If you plan on just tossing them on and not actually testing the audio, go for it. They work. But for the price, they should handle music and calls equally well. They do not.

Overall, I will have to say I was rather disappointed with these. I also reviewed their behind the neck version (Jabra Evolve 65e UC) and was hoping I had just gotten a dud with that set. Well lightening either struck twice, or the audio on these is even worse than the cheaper behind the neck version. Darn, because I wanted to love these. I have a soft spot for gadgets with cool features. These had potential. I will give them three stars because if the price point wasn’t so high, they would be okay. Not great, but they’d get the job done. I also really liked the ambient sounds you could listen to on the app. A nice little extra that was unexpected.

Hope that helps!
text_fidelity_b: Jabra Evolve 65t True Wireless Bluetooth Earbuds, UC Optimized – Superior Call Quality and Connectivity – Passive Noise Cancelling Earbuds with up to 15 hours of Battery Life with Charging Case

Unfortunately you can’t buy the best reviewed and most powerful Z wave range extenders on the market because Ring does not make them compatible with their system because they want you to buy their crappy extenders of course.

I guess we should just be grateful that at least some of the compatible smart plugs have signal extenders built into them that are better than Ring’s.

Issue 2: They are dumb. The algorithms for determining what path a device takes, in terms of whether it connects to a certain range extender or the base station, is horrible. This flaw includes the range extenders themselves when they try and decide whether or not to connect to the base station or another range extender. (I have two Ring range extenders).

If you have one range extender 20-30 feet from the base station and then place another range extender 20-30 feet from the first range extender branching out in the same direction there is no guarantee that the second range extender will connect to the first range extender rather than trying to connect to the base station.

Maybe this is because the signal from the range extenders is so bad that the devices are programmed to connect to the base station if at all possible, even if the signal is weak.

One support tech even told me a “funny” story about how a friend of theirs has a range extender just fifteen feet away from the base station in their house and but the range extended chooses to connect to another range extender that is more than 40 feet away rather than directly to the base station that is just 15 feet from it.

Ha ha ha, it’s SO funny when your expensive electronic product that you bought to keep your home safe does not work correctly! Hilarious!

A secondary criticism is that if the signal to the keypad isn’t strong enough the keypad alarm might not sound.

I have two doors between my keypad and the range extender it connects to.
When the doors are open the keypad usually sounds the alarm, when they are closed it never does.

It would seem obvious to any rational person that the issue with the alarm not sounding is the signal strength but the tech support people swear up and down that that is not possible.

Even when the doors are closed the tech support people claim the keypad reads as having an adequate signals strength ( the tech support people can see the signal strength of your devices but you can’t).

They are actually sending me a new keypad but I am not hopeful it will solve the problem.
It seems obvious to me that the command for signaling the alarm requires a better signal than the other functions of the keypad.

Maybe the signal for the alarm is only sent out once while the signal for the other functions are repeatedly sent out until the base station acknowledges them? Who knows?

The point is that it seems like a design flaw and if you plan on having your keypad more than a room lengths away from your base station you shouldn't count on the alarm on the keypad working.

I will update this review with the performance of my replacement keypad.

The last thing I will say is that the price of 11 dollars a month for monitoring the entire system regardless of how many devices you have, including any cameras, is a great price.

I hope that this type of price is here to stay. If they pull a bait and switch where they significantly increase the price of monitoring after they initially get enough people to buy the system I will drop this system like a hot potato and sell it used on eBay.
text_fidelity_b: Ring Alarm 5 Piece Kit (1st Gen) – Home Security System with optional 24/7 Professional Monitoring – No long-term contracts – Works with Alexa

G.G.Martinsen Black 16 G Mini Usb Port Slim Small Multi-ling I've had the opportunity to review three different G.G. Martinsen players, and of the three this one is my favorite. I brought two of the players, pre-charged, to review at my sister's where I am staying a week while she had and recovers from surgery, and the one thing I can say right off the bat is that I wish the charging cable was of the ubiquitous Micro-A type and not the mini type, which I did not think to bring with me. The [[ASIN:B016F4AGLC other player]] handles like the [[ASIN:B0173CW2CQ first one]] I reviewed for G.G. Martinsen, but I will have to wait until I get back home to do anything other than test the recorder and FM radio on this 16GB player because I have no cable to copy music onto the player with!

Anyway, unlike the other two players, the controls on this one make sense and handle more like what I'm used to. The instructions that come with this (that I also left at home!) were well-written in English, unlike so many products coming out of China these days. But I haven't needed the instructions to figure out how to use this player or change the settings. The first thing I did was set the Power Off and Sleep settings to 0 so the player won't shut off unless I flip the manual switch to turn it off. I have been listening to this player while I've been writing reviews, and I have had absolutely no cutouts with the FM radio even though I'm in a condo sandwiched on all sides by other units and this place is bad with reception of cable TV and other radios. I like that the station stays selected even when you power the player off and on again.

The control dial is easy to see, with a top Menu button, left and right arrows, and a pause/play button on the bottom (something the other players did not have). The round button in the middle has a good tactile feel, and even in the dark it's fairly easy to feel where to press for the different functions. I'll have to re-read the instructions to understand fully when to use the center button and how.

The little piece you can thread a lanyard into is plastic, but I don't think it will break easily unless you put a lot of stress on it. The player comes with a pair of original Apple-style earphones, which are great for walking outside where you need to be able to hear sounds around you while listening to music. The headphones are not the best in the world, but they are a nice additional feature and good to have in situations where you wouldn't want pricier headphones to get ruined (the gym, outside should it start raining). Of course, your listening experience will only be as good as the wired headphones you plug into this player. It really is a whole lot of bang for the buck and an attractive little player. I have the turquoise color, and it's really nice.

I put links to the other two players I have reviewed so you can compare them. What I like about this one is it doesn't have that gimmicky bubble-gum type selection screen but, rather, just has a list of the different features and functions. The list is easy to read and looks more businesslike and professional than the more cartoonish screens of the other two players.
text_fidelity_b: G.G.Martinsen Black 16 G Mini Usb Port Slim Small Multi-ling

text_fidelity_a:
Magellan RoadMate 1470 4.7-Inch Widescreen Portable GPS Navigator I've been a Magellan user for several years - have owned four of their GPS systems, and always appreciate how they have improved their products. This unit is my 5th, and replaces a Magellan 4040. After using it for a while I've confident in saying this is the best one yet!

The most visible change is the actual size of the unit. The screen size has been increased, but the unit is thinner and lighter. Very sleek appearance, and the screen is a real joy -- sharp, clear graphics even in the sun, and bigger on-screen buttons for easy use. The mounting system has also been streamlined, and looks and works well. It mounts very easily on a NavMat holder (basically a bean-bag system that I got on Amazon. I'm a huge Navmat fan - makes it a snap to hide the GPS with narry a trace. Best accessory by far for any GPS).

The power connector was not well thought out, however. You have to connect it to the GPS unit AFTER you mount it in the holder. They should have moved the connector it a wee bit to the side to avoid that.

The only button is a slide-type power button on the top. Boot-up time is OK -- not speedy, but not a huge delay either. It does not have a "sleep" mode, so you have to do a cold boot every time. Not a problem in real world use - by the time you get situated in your car, the unit is ready to go.

Voice is clear and easy to understand. Not as natural sounding as a TomTom, but understandable.

Pretty much any recent GPS unit will get you where you want to go. I've found the routing on the Magellans to be very similar to Garmins - could be because they both use the same mapping set (Navteq). The Magellan shines, however, in features that I find helpful. The direction of the next turn is always visible regardless of how far away the next turn will be. Up until recently, Garmin did not offer this (they do now on some of their units). Sounds like a small issue, but I find it very helpful. The Magellan also allows you to very easily exclude a route (or portion). That's a fairly standard feature nowadays, but Magellan allows you to do it in a snap.

In terms of routing, Magellan offers four options (fastest, shortest, most use of freeways and least use). You can see all four options on the map (as a summary) at the same time so you can pick the best one for your needs. Perfect!!

Love the AAA Guidebook, which is a unique Magellan feature. Lets you get details about restaurants and other points of interest just like the paper version from AAA. I used it a lot in my 4040, especially when traveling out of town.

Other unique Magellan features I appreciate is the "ding dong" sound right before a turn (incredibly accurate!) and the fact that the software reminds you to "stay on the current road" when you encounter major exits. Some find that to be nagging, but it has saved me from inadvertently exiting on more than one occasion.

A new feature for Magellan is the lane guidance. Very nicely done. I've used this feature on Navigon units, and found it rather unhelpful. Magellan's implementation is far more useful, with better, clearer graphics. However, lane guidance is not available for every road.

The software is also nicely done - very logical to use. If you're a past Magellan user you can pick this up and use it in a second. If not, there's a short printed user's guide in the box (plus a CD-ROM with more in-depth info) that gets you up to speed quickly. The box also includes the mount, power connector for the car, and a USB cable. It does not include an AC adapter.

OK, now for the bad news. When it comes to customer service, Magellan has been horrid. We're talking so bad it's almost funny. I'm hoping this situation will change - the company was bought by Mitac late last year, and perhaps this will signal a change for the better in terms of customer support. Lord knows, they couldn't get any worse.

The leader, in my opinion, for customer support is Garmin. They are nice to deal with on the phone, answer emails promptly, and offer regular firmware updates. Whenever I buy a GPS as a gift I always buy Garmin since I don't want to saddle the recipient with the miserable service that Magellan offers. It's a shame, since Magellan offers some real benefits over Garmin, and more value for the money. Tom Tom is also decent when it comes to support, but they use TeleAtlas maps which are less complete than NavTeq (sp?).

Bottom line -- if you're looking for a straightforward GPS at a good price, this should be on your short list. It lacks features such as Bluetooth and an MP3 player, but for me, I want a GPS to offer guidance and not entertainment. This has a very robust feature set, great screen, and well-designed software. It also has traffic capabilities -- did not test that feature out, so I can't comment on it.

The "safe" bet continues to be Garmin. You'll pay a bit more, and get less features, but you can be assured of solid support. Whether Magellan's new owners will put them back on the right track (if you'll excuse the horrid, but unavoidable pun) in terms of customer service is not yet clear. I hope so -- they make a great product!

UPDATE: 5/21/09 There's a firmware update on the Magellan site. No new functionality (in terms of new features) but, according to the release notes it improves overall performance. Easy to install - just follow the included step-by-step instructions. It seems like it makes the unit a bit faster, but that could just be my imagination.
text_fidelity_b: Magellan RoadMate 1470 4.7-Inch Widescreen Portable GPS Navigator

text_fidelity_a:
Kindle E-reader, 6" Glare-Free Touchscreen Display, Wi-Fi - Includes Special Offers (Previous Generation – 7th) I love reading, but I am consumed by a digital age. I spend so much time playing video games and on social media, I hardly give myself the time to sit down with a good book.

I have a phone, a computer, and a tablet, each with access to the kindle app, but the lights can often cause extreme fatigue when reading for long periods of time.
I could pick up physical copies of books and read those, but often times the font is too small for my bad eyesight, and larger books can be hard to read due to the pages curving.

Enter the Kindle. This ingenious little device fixes every problem I have experienced with digital and physical reading.
Because it does not light up, I do not experience the same fatigue as when reading on my other devices.
I have the ability to increase font size all the way to the point of each letter being about 1/2" tall. The flat design makes it easy to read in any position, I can even put it on a tablet stand and read hands-free!

It is extremely light-weight and does not cause my arms to become tired like large hardcover books do in some positions.

The library of books is incredible! I can read almost any book I want, though there are many that are not yet on the kindle store.

The battery life is phenomenal. I haven't charged it in 2 months and am just now getting a low battery alert! It takes a standard MicroUSB connection.

Over all, this is an excellent device and encourages reading in the digital age.
text_fidelity_b: Kindle E-reader, 6" Glare-Free Touchscreen Display, Wi-Fi - Includes Special Offers (Previous Generation – 7th)

VIDBOX Video Conversion Suite It's been a while since I set up one of these, but it works pretty much just like I remember. You install your drivers and software, and plug this into your computer via USB and into your video source via composite cables or an s-cable. You play your source, while you record on your computer, and the file gets saved as a .mov (quicktime) file. The resolution over a composite connection gets only so good, but this is an excellent product for the price.

The only videotapes I still have are home movies, so I do not know whether you can copy your old store bought tapes to this to load onto your iPod. Loading home movies from an old camcorder worked great. I did do a quick google check and learned that this will record just about anything you can put over an analog cable, so bear that in mind if you are looking to preserve your purchased videos. To convert to an iPod-friendly format, I highly recommend iSquint. It's free and fast and easy.

That said, I'm fairly disappointed in the lack of options when using this frame. Can't use it vertically, and photos that are vertical get distorted when displayed, which sucks. text_fidelity_a:
WD 1TB Silver My Passport for Mac Portable External Hard Drive - USB 3.0 - WDBLUZ0010BSL-NESN Beside myself with joy. Backing up 775,000+ files with Time Machine could not have been easier.

This external drive was recommended by an Apple technician whom I hired to come tidy up the many issues that had developed over several years of working with my several Apple devices. While he was here, we called up Amazon and found the drive he recommended -- this one. It was promptly delivered. Connecting and running it could not have been easier. Feeling much more confident about continuing to work on my ancient MacBook.

UPDATE: This little guy has fallen on the tile flooring more times than I can count now. Amazingly, it hasn't broken yet. You should be aware that the connection to the cord that leads to your USB port is kind of loose -- especially where it plugs into the external drive. IO've had to use Scotch tape to secure it. Inelegant, but useful, BECAUSE...

Yesterday the client's gigantic file, replete with uncompressed images, crashed not only the file but my entire MS Wyrd program. Thanks to this little hard drive and Time Machine, Word was backed up -- although I didn't need to use the back-up to recover Word, the back-up could have been a life-saver. Time Machine failed to back up an uncorrupted version of the file recent enough to contain the six or eight hours' worth of edits I'd entered during that session. Ohhhh well... Not a function of the drive: a function of Apple's Time Machine.

I plan to buy another of these drives and manually back up current files, so as to have more than one copy of key data, one of which will always be unplugged from the machine.
///////

ADDENDUM: Made in Thailand, this little guy is tougher than one would expect. Because of a back problem, I can't sit at a desk; so, the external drive has been attached to a MacBook that allows me to work in pain-free seating. This entails my hauling the computer array around with me to more than one seating arrangement, and lifting the junk on and off of various nearby tables. I've dropped it several times and each time expected it would be dead. No: it survived a half-dozen drops on tile floor before I figured out that I could tape the cable into the Passport connection. Last night, though, a fairly mild tap (not a drop!) did it in. I'm ordering two more, so that I can switch them out every other day; that way, the next time I break one, I'll have a backup to the backup.

The connection between the USB cable and the Passport comes apart readily. You can remedy that -- not aesthetically but effectively -- with a piece of Scotch tape.
text_fidelity_b: WD 1TB Silver My Passport for Mac Portable External Hard Drive - USB 3.0 - WDBLUZ0010BSL-NESN

iPad Gen 5 charged from 35% to 100% in closer to 3.5 hours. I dozed off. Sorry, but I did do it again in almost the same simulation and got the same result.
